ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Gauging | San Diego, CA
ut.description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in San Diego for shipyard steel, pressure vessels, piping and storage tanks. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in San Diego, California
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to San Diego sites for ultrasonic thickness testing, corrosion surveys and ultrasonic weld inspection on carbon steel, low-alloy steel and stainless components. Typical jobs are hull and tank plate at a shipyard, process and utility piping, pressure vessels, and structural steel on piers and cranes. You send the drawings, the code and the locations; we reply within one business day. Request a UT quote for San Diego.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in San Diego

San Diego is a working waterfront. The Port of San Diego lists six shipyards on the bay, among them Austal USA, BAE Systems San Diego Ship Repair, Continental Maritime, General Dynamics NASSCO, Marine Group Boat Works and Nielsen Beaumont Marine, and they build, repair and maintain both commercial vessels and U.S. Navy ships. That puts a great deal of steel plate in one place: shell plating, tank boundaries, ballast and fuel tanks, decks, bulkheads, foundations and piping systems. Ultrasonic thickness readings are how an owner or a repair planner learns how much of that steel is left before docking, before a steel renewal estimate is written, or before a coating system is specified.

Away from the water, the same method serves the region's utilities and process users: natural gas and water piping, desalination and water-treatment plumbing, compressed-air receivers, boiler and hot-water systems in hospitals, hotels and food plants, bulk fuel and water storage tanks, and the fabrication shops that supply defense and aerospace customers. Steel highway and rail structures in the county add a bridge and structural-steel element. Each of these asset types asks a slightly different question of the same instrument, which is why a San Diego UT scope should be written around the question, not around the method.

What ultrasonic thickness testing finds, and what it misses

A thickness gauge sends a short pulse of sound through the wall and times the echo from the back surface. Because the velocity in steel is known, the instrument converts that time to thickness. The result is a single wall-thickness reading under the probe, which is exactly what a corrosion survey needs. Done at a grid of points, or at fixed condition monitoring locations, the readings show where metal has been lost and how quickly.

The method has limits that matter in a salt-air city like San Diego. Pitting is the first: a probe sitting over the shoulder of a pit reads the sound wall around it and can miss the pit entirely, so surveys on pitted plate use a denser grid or a scan of the suspect area. Heavy scale or flaking coating changes coupling and produces unstable readings, which is why surface preparation is part of the scope. Laminations in plate make the reading jump to a shallow value that is a real internal reflector, not a thin wall. Finally, thickness readings measure remaining wall; they do not size cracks, and they say nothing about coating condition. When the concern is surface-breaking cracking at a weld toe, magnetic particle testing or liquid penetrant testing answers it more directly.

Ultrasonic weld inspection with angle beams

For welds the technician uses a shear-wave probe on a wedge, usually at 45, 60 or 70 degrees, and scans from both sides of the joint where geometry allows. A reference level, or a distance-amplitude curve built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, sets the sensitivity. The technician looks for lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, cracks and slag, then characterizes each reflector by position, length, amplitude and behavior as the probe moves. Acceptance comes from the construction code, not from the instrument: a reflector that is acceptable in one standard can be rejectable in another.

Plain truths apply here. Coarse-grained castings and some stainless weld metal scatter sound and need a procedure demonstrated on a representative block. Thin plate leaves little room for the beam to resolve a flaw. Geometry such as a tight fillet or a stiffener close to the weld can block access to one side. When a weld cannot be fully covered, the report says so instead of implying coverage that was not achieved.

Codes and acceptance criteria used on San Diego work

Which document governs depends on what the steel is. For new pressure equipment, ASME Section V sets the examination methods: Article 4 for ultrasonic examination of welds and Article 5 for ultrasonic examination of materials, with the contact thickness practice in Article 23 (SE-797). ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 12 covers ultrasonic examination of welds in vessels. Process piping under ASME B31.3 refers to paragraph 344.6 for ultrasonic examination and to Table 341.3.2 for acceptance. Structural steel is governed by AWS D1.1, which carries its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and state bridge steel by AWS D1.5.

In service, the owner works to API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for aboveground storage tanks. Under those codes the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection program, and Atlantis supplies the examination data: thickness at the monitoring locations, location maps, and weld findings. ASTM E797 is the practice for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement and ASTM E164 covers contact ultrasonic examination of weldments. Work on Navy ships follows the Navy's own technical requirements and the contract specification, and the scope must name that document before a procedure is written.

California's pressure vessel regime

California regulates boilers and certain tanks through the Cal/OSHA Pressure Vessel Unit under Labor Code sections 7620 to 7771. Permits to operate are required for air tanks above 1.5 cubic feet, LP-gas storage tanks above 125 gallons water capacity, and power boilers above 15 psig steam pressure. Inspections are done by a Pressure Vessel Unit inspector or by a qualified inspector employed by an insurance company, and the regulations sit in Title 8, sections 450 to 560 for unfired pressure vessels and 750 to 797 for boilers and fired pressure vessels. The unit's Santa Ana office serves the southern counties.

Atlantis does not issue permits and is not the state inspector. What a UT scope contributes is the underlying wall-thickness evidence that the owner, the insurer's inspector or the state inspector can use when judging a vessel's condition. Ask whoever holds the permit what thickness data they want and where, then put that into the scope. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 adds a mechanical integrity requirement for covered process facilities, and thickness trending is one common way owners meet it.

How the thickness survey is carried out

The technician starts with a calibration check on a step block of the same material, with steps that bracket the expected thickness. On corroded or pitted metal a dual-element probe is the normal choice because its angled transmit and receive crystals read through rough surfaces better than a single element. An A-scan display is preferred over a simple digital readout so the technician can see doubled echoes on thin wall or a laminar reflection, both of which a number alone would hide. On hot piping the technician uses a high-temperature probe and couplant rated for the surface, and corrects the velocity for temperature where the procedure requires it.

Locations are marked on the component or on an isometric so the same points can be read again. Surface grinding or wire-brushing removes scale where needed, and the technician records the as-found surface condition next to each reading. If the owner uses condition monitoring locations, readings are taken at the same marked points each campaign so corrosion rate is calculated from comparable data. Where a point reads below the minimum, it is flagged at the time so the owner can decide whether to continue, stop or call for an engineering evaluation.

Who does the work in San Diego

Atlantis has no office in San Diego. Crews travel to your site for the scope you agree and are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the examination and interprets the results; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. For San Diego scopes, the approving Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A the written practice belongs to the employer, so technicians' qualification records are kept to that practice and are available for the owner or the authorized inspector to review. The company's management systems are certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

If your own contract requires a particular qualification scheme, state it in the request. A shipyard specification, a utility's standard and a state DOT can each ask for more than SNT-TC-1A, and the quote should reflect that before any technician is sent to site.

What the UT report contains

  • Component identification, drawing or isometric reference, and the examination location map.
  • Procedure number and revision, the governing code and the acceptance criteria used.
  • Instrument, probe and couplant details, calibration block and calibration check records.
  • Technician name and qualification level, with the Level III who approved the procedure.
  • For thickness work: a grid or location table with nominal, minimum and as-measured values, plus surface condition notes.
  • For weld work: indication location, length, amplitude or depth, accept or reject against the named criterion, and any area not covered.
  • Limitations, such as access, temperature or surface condition, stated plainly.

Planning a UT job in San Diego

San Diego's mild climate makes the instrument's life easy. Couplant behaves, and probes and cables are not fighting cold. The weather still shapes the work. Marine-layer mornings leave steel damp and salted, so surfaces need drying and cleaning before readings. Summer sun can push an exposed deck or tank shell well above what a standard probe tolerates, which calls for a high-temperature probe or shaded, early work. Santa Ana wind events carry dust that gets into couplant.

Access is the other half. Shipyard and port work usually means badging, safety orientation and gate procedures, and work inside tanks adds confined-space permits and ventilation. Dry-dock or pier schedules set when steel can be reached, and coatings crews often follow right behind the gauging crew, so UT is generally planned just before surface preparation. Tell us the site type, the permits you expect, the working window and who controls access, and travel is planned from that information.

UT, MT or PT for your San Diego job

Pick the method by the question. Use ultrasonic testing when the question is how much wall remains, or whether a weld contains an internal flaw. Use magnetic particle inspection when you need surface and near-surface cracks found quickly on carbon or low-alloy steel, such as weld toes on crane or pad-eye attachments. Use dye penetrant inspection for surface-breaking defects on non-magnetic material such as stainless piping or aluminum. Many jobs combine them: thickness readings to size the corrosion, MT on repair welds, and PT on stainless components. For a deeper view of the method itself, read the national ultrasonic testing page and the ultrasonic testing guide, or see the California inspection services hub.

Training your own technicians in ultrasonic testing

If you would rather build in-house capability, Atlantis runs UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with the Practical NDT ultrasonic testing simulator for practice between sessions. Under SNT-TC-1A your company, not a course provider, qualifies and certifies its technicians; our courses cover the classroom and practical-skills side of that program. See the San Diego NDT training page, the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker, and NDT practice tests. If your written practice needs drafting, our written practice development service covers it.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic testing cost in San Diego?
faq.a: There is no list fee, because scope drives the work: number of locations, access, surface condition, code and travel. Send drawings and locations through the quote link and a written quotation follows after review.

faq.q: Can UT measure wall thickness on a ship hull or tank while the vessel is in service?
faq.a: Often yes from outside, if the surface is accessible and cleanable. Tank interiors, coatings and heavy scale change the plan, and any hull work should be coordinated with the yard or vessel owner so access and safety controls are in place.

faq.q: What is the difference between ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection?
faq.a: Thickness testing uses a straight-beam probe to measure remaining wall. Weld inspection uses an angle-beam shear-wave probe, calibrated to a reference level, to look for internal flaws such as lack of fusion, and the results are judged against a code acceptance criterion.

faq.q: Do you perform UT on Navy vessels in San Diego?
faq.a: Navy work is controlled by the Navy's technical publications and the contract specification. If your scope names those documents and permits our personnel to work, we will quote against them; otherwise we will tell you what is missing before travel is planned.

faq.q: Which codes apply to UT of pressure vessels and piping in California?
faq.a: Construction uses ASME Section VIII and B31.3 with Section V examination articles, and in-service work follows API 510 or API 570. California adds Cal/OSHA permit and inspection rules, so confirm with the permit holder what thickness data they expect.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a San Diego office?
faq.a: No. Our people travel out to your site for each job. That lets us quote travel honestly and avoids claiming a presence we do not have, and we do not promise a specific arrival time.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing find cracks at weld toes?
faq.a: Angle-beam UT can detect cracking in a weld, but weld-toe and other surface-breaking cracks are usually found faster and more clearly with magnetic particle testing on steel or penetrant testing on non-magnetic metals. We pair methods where the question calls for it.

faq.q: What surface preparation is needed before UT?
faq.a: The surface must be clean enough for stable coupling: loose scale, rust flakes and blistered coating removed, and a smooth patch where the probe sits. Thickness through sound coating is possible with the right procedure, but heavy or damaged coating needs removal.

faq.q: Who qualifies your ultrasonic technicians?
faq.a: Technicians are qualified under Atlantis' written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with an ASNT NDT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. If your contract requires a different scheme, say so in your request so we can confirm before quoting.

faq.q: Can my own staff learn UT instead of hiring an inspection crew?
faq.a: Yes. We offer UT Level 1 and Level 2 training and a simulator for practice. Your employer's written practice governs qualification, so plan on supervised experience hours alongside coursework before anyone works unsupervised.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in San Diego, CA
mt.description: Mag particle testing in San Diego for ship and pier steel, crane and rigging welds, pressure equipment and fabricated structures. Request an MT quote today.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in San Diego, California
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to San Diego sites for magnetic particle inspection of welds, castings, forgings and in-service steel. The method is fast, sensitive and visual: it shows surface cracks and shallow subsurface flaws in carbon and low-alloy steel as bright or colored lines you can see and photograph. If you have a repair weld, a lifting attachment, a pressure-vessel nozzle or a structural connection that needs a crack check, request an MT quote for San Diego and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in San Diego

The bay's yards, piers and cranes create steady demand for crack checks. Shipyard steel gets cut, fitted and re-welded during repair periods, and every structural repair weld, pad eye, lifting lug, foundation and tank-boundary attachment is a place where fatigue or lack of fusion can start a crack. Container and breakbulk cranes, mobile cranes, forklifts and other lifting equipment operating around the port have highly stressed welds at booms, outriggers and hook blocks. Rigging hardware, shackles, hooks and spreader beams are ferromagnetic and often inspected by magnetic particle examination as part of an owner's lifting-gear program.

Inland, the method serves fabrication shops that supply the defense, aerospace and energy sectors, and pressure-equipment repair shops. It is also the standard surface check for structural steel connections, trailer and truck frames, and rail components. In every case the question is the same: is there a crack open to the surface, or just under it, that will grow under load?

What MT detects and what it cannot

Magnetic particle inspection works because a crack in a magnetized ferromagnetic part interrupts the magnetic field and pushes some flux out into the air at the crack. Fine iron particles applied to the surface are drawn to that leakage and outline the discontinuity. The part must therefore be ferromagnetic: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic or ferritic stainless grades qualify, while austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys and titanium do not respond. On those materials the method is liquid penetrant testing.

Sensitivity is highest for surface-breaking cracks and falls off quickly with depth, so MT is described as a surface and slightly subsurface method. Orientation matters: a crack is best revealed when the magnetic field crosses it at close to a right angle, which is why two field directions are applied. Heavy paint, thick weld spatter, scale and oil reduce particle mobility, and very rough weld profiles create false indications that must be evaluated. MT does not size depth or measure wall thickness; if a crack indication is found and depth matters, the engineer decides whether to grind it out, repair it or call for another method.

Techniques used on San Diego jobs

For most field work the technician uses an electromagnetic yoke, which sits across the weld and induces the field between its legs. An AC yoke is the common choice for surface cracks, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke gives deeper penetration where required. Under ASME Section V Article 7 an AC yoke must show a lifting power of at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and the technician proves it with a standard weight before the job. Prods are used where yoke access is poor, with attention to arc burns on the surface.

Particles come in two main forms. Dry powder and visible wet particles in contrasting paint are practical for outdoor and shipboard work. Fluorescent wet particles give the highest sensitivity but need UV-A light and a darkened area, which on a dock or open deck means a portable black-out tent. The technician checks the examination with a field indicator or a reference shim to confirm the field is strong enough and in the right direction, then examines the surface in two roughly perpendicular directions so cracks in any orientation are caught.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 7 sets the magnetic particle method, and ASTM E709 is the guide to the practice, with ASTM E1444 as the practice for magnetic particle testing. Acceptance depends on the job. For pressure vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 6 covers magnetic particle methods and acceptance. For process piping, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 describes the examination and Table 341.3.2 gives acceptance. Structural steel falls under AWS D1.1, and bridge steel under AWS D1.5, with visual and MT acceptance criteria written for each weld class.

In service, the owner's inspection code controls: API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping, and API 653 for tanks. The owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the program, and Atlantis performs the examination and reports the indications. Lifting equipment is examined to the manufacturer's requirements, the owner's lifting-gear program and the applicable OSHA and ASME rules, and the scope should name them.

California and the state boiler and pressure vessel rules

The Cal/OSHA Pressure Vessel Unit regulates boilers and certain tanks in California under Labor Code sections 7620 to 7771. Permits are required for air tanks above 1.5 cubic feet, LP-gas storage tanks above 125 gallons water capacity, and power boilers operating above 15 psig. Inspection is done by the unit's inspectors or by qualified insurance-company inspectors, and the rules are in Title 8, sections 450 to 560 and 750 to 797.

When a repair weld has been made on a permitted vessel, the repair itself follows the National Board Inspection Code and the owner's quality program, and the magnetic particle record is part of the evidence package. Atlantis does not act as the state or insurer inspector. If you tell us which inspector holds the permit and what record they want, the MT report can be organized to match it.

Demagnetization, cleaning and what happens after the exam

Residual magnetism can cause problems. A magnetized part can attract steel chips, interfere with arc welding by deflecting the arc, or upset nearby instruments. The procedure states whether demagnetization is required, and when it is, the technician uses a yoke or coil to reduce the residual field and checks it with a field meter. Wet particle residue is cleaned off, and any marks used to locate indications are removed or recorded on the report.

Indications are classified as relevant or non-relevant according to the code. A relevant linear indication is evaluated against the acceptance criteria, and the technician marks it, photographs it and records its length and location. Rejectable indications go back to the owner, the welding engineer or the authorized inspector for disposition. After repair, the area is re-examined with the same method.

Who performs and reviews the work

Atlantis has no office in San Diego. Technicians travel to your site and perform MT under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The Level II sets up the equipment, performs the exam and interprets indications; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The Level III behind San Diego MT scopes is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. The qualification records stay available for the owner to audit. Quality and environmental management at Atlantis carry ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certificates.

Because SNT-TC-1A is an employer-based recommended practice, the employer writes the details. If your contract requires a specific qualification route, or a procedure approved by your own Level III, say so when you request a quote.

What the MT report contains

  • Component identification, location, drawing or sketch, and examination date.
  • Procedure number and revision, governing code and acceptance criteria.
  • Equipment: yoke type and serial number, lifting-power check, UV-A meter and ambient light readings if fluorescent.
  • Particles and carrier, surface condition and the technique used.
  • Technician name and level, with the Level III approval.
  • Each indication with location, length and orientation, photographed, with accept or reject.
  • Demagnetization performed or not required, and any area not examined.

Planning an MT job in San Diego

The coastal climate favors the work, with moderate temperatures and little freezing. Humidity, morning fog and salt on the steel still affect particle mobility, so surfaces must be dry and clean. Direct sun on a deck or tank shell can heat the surface enough to dry the carrier too fast, and a bright day makes visible indications easier but fluorescent work harder, which is why shaded or tented areas are planned for fluorescent examination. Wind blows dry powder away, so dry powder is a poorer choice on open piers.

Shipyard, port and plant work usually needs gate badging, safety orientation and permits for hot work or confined spaces nearby. MT needs access to the weld and clearance around it for the yoke, so scaffolding, staging and lighting should be arranged before the technician arrives. Tell us the component type, surface condition, expected permits and working window, and we will plan travel and equipment from that information.

One more practical point for San Diego repair work: earthquake exposure and heavy equipment use mean owners sometimes call for a crack check after an unusual load event, such as a crane overload or a hard grounding. An MT survey of the critical welds is a sensible first screen in those cases, and it is far easier to plan if the weld locations and the event description arrive with the request.

MT, PT or UT for your San Diego job

Use magnetic particle inspection for steel when the concern is a surface or near-surface crack. Choose penetrant testing for stainless steel, aluminum or other non-magnetic metals. Choose ultrasonic testing when you need wall thickness or an internal weld flaw found, since MT cannot see below the surface. A typical San Diego repair package may use all three: ultrasonic thickness readings to size the loss, MT on repair welds and PT on stainless attachments. Read more on the national magnetic particle testing page, the complete MT guide, the MT versus PT comparison, and the California inspection hub.

Training your own MT technicians

Many owners with steady crack-check needs prefer to train in-house. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, plus broader magnetic particle testing training. Your employer's written practice governs qualification, so supervised experience hours remain essential. See the San Diego NDT training page and the ASME Section V Article 7 explained.

faq.q: What materials can magnetic particle inspection be used on?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic materials: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic or ferritic stainless grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys and titanium do not hold a magnetic field, so those parts need penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: How deep can magnetic particle testing find a crack?
faq.a: MT finds surface-breaking cracks and flaws just beneath the surface, with sensitivity dropping quickly with depth. It cannot size crack depth, so a rejectable indication goes to an engineer or authorized inspector for disposition.

faq.q: Is MT suitable for crane and rigging inspection in San Diego?
faq.a: Yes, MT is a standard crack check for crane booms, pad eyes, hooks and rigging hardware made of ferromagnetic steel. The scope should state the owner's lifting-gear program, the manufacturer's requirements and any applicable ASME or OSHA rules.

faq.q: Wet fluorescent or dry powder: which is used for field work?
faq.a: Dry powder and visible wet particles suit outdoor and shipboard work. Fluorescent wet particles give higher sensitivity but need UV-A light and a darkened area, so we plan a tent or an indoor setup where that method is required.

faq.q: Does the part need to be demagnetized after MT?
faq.a: Only when the procedure or the next operation calls for it. Residual magnetism can attract chips, deflect a welding arc or disturb instruments, so we check the field with a meter and demagnetize when required.

faq.q: How are magnetic particle indications judged?
faq.a: Against the acceptance criteria in the governing code, such as ASME Section VIII Appendix 6, ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 or AWS D1.1. Relevant linear indications are measured and recorded, and the owner or engineer decides on repair.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have staff stationed in San Diego?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and we quote travel on the specifics of your job. We do not promise a specific arrival time before access, permits and scope are confirmed.

faq.q: Can MT be done through paint?
faq.a: Thin, well-bonded coatings can sometimes be examined, but thickness limits and procedure qualification apply, and sensitivity drops. Thick, flaking or damaged paint should be removed locally before the examination.

faq.q: What qualifications do your MT technicians hold?
faq.a: They are qualified under Atlantis' written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with an ASNT NDT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. If your contract requires another scheme, tell us in the request so we can confirm it first.

faq.q: Can my employees be trained to do MT themselves?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and Level 2 training, and your company's written practice then governs qualification and the experience hours required before independent work.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in San Diego, CA
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in San Diego for stainless, aluminum and nickel-alloy welds and castings, per ASME Section V Article 6. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in San Diego, California
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to San Diego sites for liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection. The method finds cracks, laps, porosity and seams that are open to the surface of almost any non-porous material, which makes it the crack check for stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys and bronze, where magnetic methods do not work. Send the part or weld description and the governing code through the quote link and we reply within one business day: request a PT quote for San Diego.

Where penetrant testing fits in San Diego

San Diego's industrial base leans toward marine, defense and aerospace work, and much of that hardware is not magnetic. Vessels working in salt water use stainless piping, aluminum structure and superstructure, copper-nickel seawater systems, bronze valves and propulsion components, and titanium in some systems. Shipyards repairing or modifying those systems weld them, and repair welds on non-magnetic material are typical penetrant jobs. Fabrication and machine shops that supply defense, aerospace and medical-device customers use penetrant testing on machined parts, castings, weldments and tubing.

The region's process and utility users add stainless and alloy piping in water treatment and desalination, food and beverage plants, biotech and pharmaceutical facilities, and hot-water systems. Welds on sanitary or corrosive-service stainless are often penetrant-tested because a surface crack there is both a leak path and a corrosion starter. The method also serves as a check on ground-out weld repairs in carbon steel, where the repair area is small and the surface is clean.

What penetrant testing finds and what it cannot

Liquid penetrant testing works by capillary action. A low-viscosity liquid, red dye or fluorescent, is applied to a clean, dry surface and given time to enter any opening. The surface is then cleaned, a developer is applied, and the developer draws penetrant back out of the discontinuity so it shows as a colored or glowing line or dot. The size of the bleed-out is larger than the flaw itself, which is why the method is sensitive to very tight cracks.

The limits are practical. Only discontinuities that are open to the surface can be found, so a subsurface flaw is invisible. Anything that closes the opening defeats the test: heavy grinding or peening smears metal across a crack, shot or sand blasting can peen it shut, and paint, rust, oil and weld spatter block the entry. Rough or porous surfaces hold penetrant everywhere and create a background that hides indications. For cracks that may sit just under the surface of carbon steel, magnetic particle testing is quicker, and for wall thickness or internal weld flaws ultrasonic testing is required.

Penetrant systems and how they are chosen

Penetrants are classed by type and by removal method. Type II visible dye penetrants are practical in daylight on a pier or deck. Type I fluorescent penetrants are more sensitive and are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, which on site means a tent or a shaded room. Removal is by water-washable, solvent-removable or post-emulsifiable systems. Solvent-removable is the usual choice for field work because it needs only wipes and cleaner, while water-washable suits larger parts in a shop.

Material compatibility matters. On austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys, and on titanium, the penetrant materials are controlled for sulfur, chlorine and fluorine content so the test does not leave residues that could harm the part in service. The procedure should name the lot and the certification of the penetrant materials, and the report records them. A wise owner asks about this before the job when the part is for oxygen, hydrogen, seawater or high-temperature service.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 6 is the method document for liquid penetrant examination, and ASTM E165 is the standard practice for general industry. For pressure vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 8 gives methods and acceptance. In process piping, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 describes the examination and Table 341.3.2 sets acceptance. For structural and sanitary stainless welding, AWS D1.1 and AWS D1.6 may apply respectively, and the owner's specification can add further limits on indication size.

The standard temperature range for the part and the penetrant materials under Article 6 is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature. For in-service pressure equipment, API 510 and API 570 govern the program, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible, and the penetrant report is evidence the inspector can review. Aerospace and defense parts often carry their own specification, so name it in the request and we will confirm the work fits before travel is planned.

California pressure equipment rules in brief

The Cal/OSHA Pressure Vessel Unit administers California's boiler and pressure vessel rules under Labor Code sections 7620 to 7771, with the regulations in Title 8, sections 450 to 560 and 750 to 797. Operating permits apply to air tanks above 1.5 cubic feet, LP-gas storage tanks above 125 gallons water capacity and power boilers above 15 psig, and inspections are performed by unit inspectors or qualified insurance inspectors.

For a permitted vessel in San Diego County, a penetrant record of a stainless or alloy repair weld is part of the file the inspector may ask to see. Atlantis is not the state or insurance inspector, and the report is written so the person who holds that role can use it.

How a penetrant examination is performed

  1. Pre-clean the surface with solvent or approved cleaner and remove oil, grease, paint, rust and scale so the discontinuity is open. Mechanical cleaning must not smear the metal.
  2. Check the temperature of the part and the materials against the procedure range, and note it in the record.
  3. Apply the penetrant by spray, brush or wipe and keep it wet for the dwell time stated in the procedure, which depends on the material and the type of flaw expected.
  4. Remove the excess penetrant using the method in the procedure, taking care not to over-remove and wash penetrant out of a flaw.
  5. Apply a thin, even developer coat, either dry, aqueous or non-aqueous wet developer, and allow the specified development time.
  6. Examine in adequate white light, or under UV-A in a darkened area for fluorescent systems, and evaluate each indication against the acceptance criteria.
  7. Post-clean the part, especially on stainless and nickel alloys, and report.

A technician who knows the difference between a relevant indication and a false one, such as a bleed-out from a rough weld profile or scratch, is what makes the method reliable. When an indication is doubtful, the surface is cleaned and re-tested.

Who does the work and who reviews it

Atlantis has no office in San Diego. Technicians are mobilized to the work site and perform PT under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up, performs and interprets the test; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. On San Diego PT scopes that Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, holder of ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis maintains ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification across the business.

Defense and aerospace work sometimes calls for a customer-approved procedure or a named qualification route. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer writes the practice, so that requirement belongs in the request and the quote, not as a surprise on the day.

What the PT report contains

  • Part or weld identification, material and drawing reference, and examination date and location.
  • Procedure number and revision, governing code or specification, and acceptance criteria.
  • Penetrant, remover and developer brand, type, method and lot numbers, with contaminant certification where required.
  • Surface temperature, pre-cleaning method, dwell and development times.
  • Lighting: white-light intensity, or UV-A intensity and ambient light for fluorescent work.
  • Indications with location, length and type, photographed, with accept or reject.
  • Technician name and level, with the Level III approval, plus any area not examined.

Planning a PT job in San Diego

San Diego's weather is helpful. Most of the year the metal sits well inside the 40 to 125 degree window, and there is no winter freeze to stop a job. The risks are specific. Sun on a steel deck or aluminum panel in summer can push surface temperature past 125, and a hot surface dries penetrant too quickly. Humid mornings and marine fog leave moisture that must be removed before pre-cleaning, and coastal wind carries salt and dust onto a wet developer coat. Plan the work for the cooler part of the day and use shade or a tent.

Access and housekeeping matter more than weather. Penetrant materials are chemicals, and ship, port and plant sites have rules for solvents, waste and hot work nearby. Cleaner and rags must be handled under the site's safety program, and work inside tanks needs confined-space controls. Let us know the surface condition, the material and the permit requirements, and we will plan the materials and travel accordingly.

Documentation deserves a moment in San Diego defense and marine work, where records follow the part for years. Photograph each indication beside a scale, record the lot numbers of every penetrant material, and keep the cleaning steps in the report. When a part moves between shops, that record is what lets the next inspector trust the result without repeating the test.

PT, MT or UT for your San Diego job

Choose penetrant testing for non-magnetic metals or when the geometry rules out a yoke, and when the concern is a crack that is open to the surface. Choose magnetic particle inspection for carbon and low-alloy steel when speed matters and a shallow subsurface flaw is possible. Choose ultrasonic testing when wall thickness or internal flaws are the issue. Learn the method in the national penetrant testing page, the MT versus PT comparison, the ASME Section V Article 6 explainer, and the California inspection hub.

Training your own PT technicians

If you do enough surface testing to justify staff, Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training, PT Level 2 training and general penetrant testing training, with the penetrant testing simulator for practice. Your company's written practice sets qualification and the experience hours before independent work. See the San Diego NDT training page and Level III consulting if you need procedures written or approved.

faq.q: What is dye penetrant inspection used for in San Diego?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks, porosity, laps and seams in non-magnetic and non-porous materials, such as stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys common in marine, defense and process work. Subsurface flaws cannot be found by penetrant.

faq.q: Can liquid penetrant testing be used on carbon steel?
faq.a: Yes, penetrant works on any non-porous material, including carbon steel. For ferromagnetic steel, magnetic particle inspection is often faster and also shows shallow subsurface flaws, so we recommend the method that suits the question.

faq.q: What temperature range is allowed for penetrant testing?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 gives a standard range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the penetrant materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, and the record notes the surface temperature.

faq.q: Why does grinding or blasting matter before penetrant testing?
faq.a: Mechanical cleaning can smear or peen metal over a crack and close its opening, which hides the flaw. Chemical or light cleaning is preferred, and etching may be required to reopen surfaces that have been worked.

faq.q: Is there a concern about contaminants on stainless or nickel alloys?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant materials used on austenitic stainless, nickel alloys and titanium are controlled for sulfur, chlorine and fluorine. We record the material lots and cleaning steps so the owner can show the part was handled correctly.

faq.q: Do you work on Navy or defense parts in San Diego?
faq.a: If your specification names the procedure and permits our personnel on the job, we will quote against it. Please include the document in the request so we can confirm the work fits before technicians are mobilized.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a San Diego office or lab?
faq.a: No. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. We quote travel on the actual job details and do not promise a specific arrival time.

faq.q: Visible or fluorescent penetrant: which is better?
faq.a: Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive but needs UV-A light and a darkened area. Visible dye works in daylight and is easier on a pier or deck. The code, the part and the site conditions decide which is used.

faq.q: What qualifications do your PT technicians hold?
faq.a: They are qualified under Atlantis' written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with an ASNT NDT Level III approving procedures and reviewing the report. If your contract names a different scheme, say so in your request.

faq.q: Can my team learn penetrant testing instead of hiring a crew?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 and Level 2 training and a simulator. Qualification itself is set by your employer's written practice, including the experience hours before independent work.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in San Diego, CA | UT Options
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For San Diego welds, ask about UT, Level III review of existing radiographs, or RT theory training.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in San Diego, California
rt.html:
If you searched for radiographic testing in San Diego, you should know up front: Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States. Industrial radiography here is a licensed activity. Sources of radiation are regulated under U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules, 10 CFR Part 34, or the equivalent rules of Agreement States such as California, and it is not a service Atlantis offers. What we can do for a San Diego owner, contractor or engineer is listed below.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative

Radiography is often specified because a weld needs a volumetric examination, meaning a look through the full thickness and not just at the surface. Ultrasonic testing can provide that on many welds, and Atlantis mobilizes technicians to San Diego sites to do it: see our ultrasonic testing in San Diego page. The key point is that substitution is not ours to decide. Some codes allow ultrasonic examination of production welds in place of radiography. ASME B31.3 contains provisions for ultrasonic examination, API 1104 provides for ultrasonic examination of pipeline girth welds under its own conditions, AWS D1.1 has acceptance criteria for ultrasonic testing of groove welds, and ASME Section VIII Division 1 allows ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only under specific conditions.

Because of that, the change should be agreed before the job by the owner, the design engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector. Send us the code, the joint types and thicknesses, and the acceptance criteria in your contract, and we will tell you plainly whether ultrasonic examination fits, what it can and cannot show, and what a procedure demonstration would need. Ultrasonic testing is not a like-for-like image: it gives a different kind of evidence, and some flaw types and geometries favor one method over the other.

ASNT Level III radiography services that need no radiation license

A great deal of radiography quality work happens away from the source. Reviewing images and paperwork does not require handling a radiation source, and the founder of Atlantis, Anoop Rayavarapu, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. For San Diego owners and contractors this covers:

  • Independent review of radiographs, whether film or digital images, and their technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code.
  • A second read on disputed or borderline indications before a repair or rejection decision is made.
  • Review of a radiography contractor's procedure and written practice, including whether it meets the contract and the code.
  • Audit of radiographic records, such as image quality indicator use, density or exposure records and reader qualification documents.

This is review and consulting work done from the records. It does not involve exposing a component or handling a radioactive source, and it complements, but does not replace, the work of a licensed radiography contractor. If you need a contractor, your own procurement process should select one.

Radiographic testing training

If you want to understand the method or build in-house capability, theory training is available through our radiographic testing Level 2 course. Radiation safety training and the licensing needed to handle sources are separate matters that sit with the regulator and licensed providers, and our course does not replace them. Qualification under SNT-TC-1A remains the employer's responsibility, and see the San Diego NDT training page for local course information.

Next steps for your San Diego job

Tell us what you need to learn about a weld or a component: whether volumetric coverage is required, which code applies, and what your inspector will accept. We will point you to ultrasonic testing, magnetic particle inspection or dye penetrant inspection where they fit, or to a Level III review where radiographs already exist. Atlantis has no office in San Diego, technicians are mobilized to your site for agreed scope, and we reply within one business day. Ask about UT or a Level III radiograph review in San Diego.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in San Diego?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing anywhere in the United States, because industrial radiography requires a radiation license under NRC or Agreement State rules. Instead, ultrasonic testing, Level III review of existing radiographs and training are available.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my welds?
faq.a: Sometimes, if the construction code and the owner permit it. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 contain ultrasonic provisions, and Section VIII allows it only under conditions. Get owner, engineer and authorized inspector agreement before swapping methods.

faq.q: Can an ASNT Level III review radiographs I already have?
faq.a: Yes. A Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, give a second read on disputed indications and check a contractor's procedure and records.

faq.q: Where can I learn radiographic testing theory?
faq.a: A radiographic testing Level 2 course covers the theory side. It does not replace radiation safety training or any license required to handle sources, and your employer's written practice governs qualification.
